title: Purpose, tone and main idea
summary: Separate what a passage says overall, why the writer presents it and what attitude the writer's language reveals.

sections.title: Ask three different questions
content: Main idea asks: what central message does the whole passage develop? Purpose asks: what is the writer trying to do for the reader? Tone asks: what attitude does the writer reveal towards the subject?
These answers should fit together, but they are not interchangeable. A report may explain a promising experiment, evaluate its limits and maintain a cautiously positive tone.

sections.title: Build the main idea from coverage and emphasis
content: Name the topic, then add the writer's most important message about it. A topic such as a library quiet hour is too broad; a main idea must state what the passage concludes or emphasises about that initiative.

Use the coverage test: the best main idea accounts for the beginning, middle and ending. Use the emphasis test: repeated or developed evidence matters more than one vivid detail. Reject an option that is true but describes only one paragraph.

sections.title: Identify purpose through the writer's work
content: Choose a precise verb such as explain, compare, evaluate, argue, warn or entertain. Then complete the phrase: the writer aims to [verb] [what] so that the reader [understands, considers or does what].

A passage can contain facts without having the sole purpose of listing facts. If it presents results, limitations, objections and a response, its larger purpose may be to evaluate an initiative rather than merely announce it.

sections.title: Read tone from clusters, not one word
content: Underline evaluative words, degrees of certainty and any contrast. Words such as encouraging, may, however and worth refining can combine to create a cautiously positive tone.

Confirm tone with at least two signals from different parts of the passage. Do not label the tone cheerful merely because the topic is positive, or critical merely because the writer mentions a limitation.

sections.title: Use Topic, Message, Job and Attitude
content: Topic: state the subject in a few words. Message: summarise what the full passage says about it. Job: identify what the writer does with the information. Attitude: describe the writer's stance and prove it with language choices.
Before choosing an answer, compare it against the final paragraph. Conclusions often reveal the intended balance, but they must still agree with the evidence developed earlier.

sections.title: Reject three tempting distractors
content: Detail trap: the option is accurate but covers only one example. Strong-language trap: the option changes cautious evaluation into proof, condemnation or celebration. Reader-reaction trap: the option describes how you felt rather than the attitude expressed by the writer.
Revise each rejected option by naming what it misses: overall coverage, the writer's actual task, or evidence for the claimed attitude.

sections.title: The library's quiet first hour
content: Answer six questions about an original five-paragraph report. Track the central message, the writer's purpose, the tone and the role of supporting details. Feedback appears after the complete group.
